evidence.supportingExcerpt: Immunogenicity asks whether an intervention elicits an immune response; clinical efficacy asks what adding it changes in a defined clinical endpoint, population and comparison. An immune result can justify further investigation without settling whether adding the intervention improves outcomes. For a therapeutic cancer vaccine, antigen-stimulated secretion and recurrence over follow-up answer different questions. The immune result needs its specimen, stimulus, preparation, timing, controls and denominator. The clinical result needs the intervention components, comparator, outcome rule, starting clock, follow-up, missing-data handling, harms and uncertainty. A surrogate endpoint also needs evidence connecting it to clinical benefit in that setting. Comparing standard care plus vaccine with the same care without vaccine can address the addition. Randomisation strengthens attribution, while measurement quality and follow-up remain necessary. Even a clinical outcome difference does not identify the particular clone or immune mechanism that caused it. The FDA's 2018 endpoint guidance informs these general distinctions, rather than current regulatory or treatment advice.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the probability of remaining free of a defined event from a stated starting time while accounting for incomplete follow-up. At each event time, the previous estimate is multiplied by the fraction of people still at risk just before that time who avoid the event. Right censoring means observation ended without the event being seen, for example at cutoff or loss to follow-up. It leaves the current height unchanged but removes that person from later risk sets. A censor tick is neither an event nor proof of permanent event freedom. Interpretation requires censoring to be sufficiently independent of future event time within the analysis; losing contact because disease is worsening can bias the estimate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Five fictional participants start follow-up for first recurrence, with no deaths in this example. One recurrence at month 1 leaves 4/5, or 80%, recurrence-free. The example stops at month 3 and supplies no later outcome, confidence interval or individual prognosis.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A five-year curve height is an estimate from its stated origin. A landmark analysis instead selects people meeting a condition at a later time, such as being observed and event-free at month 6, then evaluates subsequent outcomes. It changes the population and clock and handles early events differently from the original trial comparison. Classifying people by a later response can also bias survival comparisons if timing is mishandled. Read the endpoint, origin, cutoff, censoring rules, confidence intervals and number-at-risk table together. At-risk counts are changing denominators, not new enrolment; a flat late tail may rest on very few people and does not establish cure. Median survival is when the curve reaches 50%; “not reached” means it did not reach that level during observed follow-up. Median follow-up describes observation time. Neither statement implies there were no events. Curve height is not a hazard ratio, and curve separation needs a suitable study design for a causal interpretation.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Treating deaths that occur before the recurrence of interest as censoring and calculating one minus Kaplan-Meier targets a different quantity from cumulative incidence and can overstate that real-world recurrence probability. Cumulative incidence addresses that competing-risk question. The nonparametric Aalen-Johansen estimator estimates state probabilities, including cumulative incidence as a competing-risk special case, under the relevant event, observation and censoring assumptions. Fine-Gray regression is a separate model for covariate effects on the subdistribution hazard. Austin and colleagues' 2016 tutorial supports the bias and hazard distinctions; Therneau, Crowson and Atkinson's September 2026 technical vignette separately supplies the Aalen-Johansen method name and its relationship to cumulative incidence. Neither estimator removes the need for an appropriate event definition and follow-up.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A surrogate is a measured outcome used in place of a direct clinical-benefit outcome, with evidence needed for that substitution in the intended setting. Two relationships must be separated: people with a favourable marker may have better outcomes, while treatments that improve that marker may or may not improve the outcome. The first is a prognostic association; the second concerns agreement between treatment effects across suitable randomised comparisons. A treatment can change another pathway, later disease or toxicity as well as the marker. Validation is specific to disease, treatment context and intended outcome. An early measure is not automatically validated, and regulatory acceptance in one programme does not transfer to another. “Validated” and “reasonably likely to predict benefit” carry different evidence claims. Even a pathology or imaging response does not capture every benefit and harm.

Participant dates, event types, follow-up status, censoring and cutoff determine the resulting curve, time-specific estimate or rate comparison and its uncertainty. An acronym or a second operation alone does not establish which events count. FDA's December 2018 nonbinding guidance discusses evidence by indication and pathway. It describes progression-free survival as able, depending on disease, context and effect size, to support accelerated approval, support traditional approval or represent direct clinical benefit. This does not universally validate it as a substitute for overall survival. A favourable distant-event endpoint does not settle local control or overall survival. An endpoint association also differs from proof that acting on a biomarker improves outcomes.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A higher percentage in one paper is a reason to examine its study, rather than proof that its treatment is better. Randomisation protects comparisons within a trial, not between separately conducted trials. Comparing their experimental arms discards that protection. Disease burden, biomarker assay and threshold, prior treatment, background care, dose, endpoint rules, analysis population and follow-up can differ. Formal indirect comparison through a common comparator preserves each trial's treatment-versus-control contrast but still requires compatible questions and methods. Pooling active arms across trials is prone to bias, and even an adjusted indirect estimate remains less secure than a suitable direct comparison (Bucher and colleagues, 1997). Network meta-analysis adds a transitivity assumption: important effect modifiers must be sufficiently comparable across the network. A shared drug name or statistical agreement cannot establish that unmeasured compatibility. Similar endpoint labels can hide different definitions: a clinical benefit rate may include different durations of stable disease. Adjustment for measured differences does not remove every bias, and lower hazard ratios against different comparators cannot automatically rank treatments.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Lead time is the interval between defined earlier and later detection events. Lead-time bias occurs when that timing difference is mistaken for a better outcome. Earlier effective intervention could help, but its benefit needs separate evidence; correcting the clock alone does not solve selection, confounding or missing follow-up.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The same timing distinction extends beyond the prostate-screening context of this record. Historical breast-cancer surveillance trials illustrate why strategy and outcome must stay together. Rosselli Del Turco and colleagues' 1994 trial enrolled 1,243 surgically treated patients with unilateral invasive breast cancer and no metastases. Adding six-monthly chest radiographs and bone scans detected more isolated intrathoracic and bone metastases, 112 versus 71, and the report described earlier detection of recurrences in that group; five-year relapse-free survival, which stops at detection, was significantly lower with intensive follow-up, while five-year mortality was 18.6% versus 19.5%, with no mortality improvement reported. The separate GIVIO trial enrolled 1,320 women and reported no overall-survival or quality-of-life difference, and no significant difference in time to recurrence detection. Thus the trials should not both be described as showing earlier detection: only the first reported it. Their results do not establish equivalence or the effects of modern imaging and treatment, and a nonsignificant comparison is not proof of exactly zero benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Growth-rate-corrected metrics in this record concern dividing-cell assays. The following fictional tumour-volume examples teach the broader distinction between growth reduction and regression; clinical RECIST assessment uses its own lesion-diameter rules. Real studies need distributions, independent units, allocation, missing observations and uncertainty. For a percentage labelled tumour growth inhibition, recover the paper's actual calculation and reference before quoting it; the fictional 70% above compares final volumes. Slower growth does not by itself identify cell death, and statistical regression is a different meaning of the word.
